flavor: They built in stone so that someone would remember them. Something did.
rules: Any civilisation, culture or people of the ancient world before about AD 500, plus those of the Americas, Africa, Asia and Oceania that flourished before about 1500. Peoples of legend and fiction don't count.

answers.lore: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
At its height, under Trajan around AD 117, its empire stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia.
The Greeks called themselves Hellenes. The name Greek comes from the Romans, who called them Graeci.
The Maya never vanished. Millions of their descendants still speak Mayan languages today.
They called themselves the Mexica, and so gave Mexico its name.
Their road network, the Qhapaq Ñan, ran for some 30,000 km through and along the Andes.
The Sumerians were among the first to write, and their counting in sixties lives on in our minutes and seconds.
Its cities had covered drains, but its script has never been deciphered.
Their alphabet is the ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets, and so of the letters you are reading.
They never called themselves Minoans. Arthur Evans named them after Minos, the king of legend.
Their Linear B script, cracked in 1952, turned out to be an early form of Greek.
Their language, written in a Greek-style alphabet, is still only partly understood.
Long known mainly from the Bible, until their lost capital was dug up in Turkey.
They carved colossal stone heads, some about three metres tall.
Their general Hannibal led an army, elephants and all, over the Alps in 218 BC.
Attila's Huns invaded Italy in 452 but turned back without taking Rome.
Their sack of Rome in AD 455 later gave us the word vandalism.
In the early 1400s Ming treasure fleets under Zheng He sailed as far as East Africa.
Sargon of Akkad built what is often called the world's first empire.
They carved Petra out of the rock and grew rich on the incense trade.
Their secret weapon, Greek fire, burned even on water. Its recipe has been lost.
Their West Baray, a reservoir at Angkor some 8 km long, was built by hand nearly a thousand years ago.
They made some of the earliest known sculptures of sub-Saharan Africa, in terracotta.
Their cultures are among the oldest continuous cultures on Earth, going back at least 50,000 years.
On a tiny island far out in the Pacific, they carved nearly a thousand moai statues.
The Romans called them Picti, the painted ones, perhaps for body paint or tattoos.
Their empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history.
Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, ending the Roman Empire in the east.
The first known mention of Arabs is an Assyrian record of 853 BC naming Gindibu the Arab, who brought 1,000 camels to the battle of Qarqar.
The Haudenosaunee, 'people of the longhouse', joined five nations under the Great Law of Peace, by tradition long before Europeans arrived.
Their Thule ancestors spread from Alaska to Greenland some 800 years ago, with dog sleds and skin boats.
Their Baghdad, founded in 762, had a House of Wisdom where Greek learning was translated into Arabic.
Seafaring raiders blamed for the fall of Bronze Age kingdoms around 1200 BC. Who they were is still argued over.
They ruled much of Iberia from 711, and their last kingdom, Granada, fell in 1492.
Their Orkhon inscriptions, carved in the 730s, are among the oldest known texts in a Turkic language.
By about 715 their caliphate stretched from Spain to the Indus.
They founded Cairo in 969.
Their victory over the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to the Turks.
Slave soldiers who took Egypt for themselves and in 1260 beat the Mongols at Ain Jalut.
Timur's heirs made Samarkand a centre of learning; part of Ulugh Beg's great observatory survives.
Its first sultan, Qutb ud-Din Aibak, began the Qutb Minar around 1199.
Its capital, Hampi, is thought to have been one of the largest cities in the world around 1500.
They carved the Kailasa temple at Ellora out of a single cliff.
They built the Shore Temple and the rock carvings of Mahabalipuram.
The Mahavamsa chronicle says Prince Vijaya founded the first Sinhalese kingdom in 543 BC, a date that belongs to legend.
Sangam poetry, the oldest Tamil literature, describes their kingdoms and their trade with Rome.
Its Buddhist sculptors gave the Buddha a Greek look, with wavy hair and flowing robes.
King Menander, the Milinda of a Buddhist dialogue, ruled from Sagala in the Punjab.
Real horsemen of the steppe, whose name Robert E. Howard later borrowed for Conan.
The Uyghur Khaganate ruled the Mongolian steppe from 744 to 840.
Its bronze masks have eyes that jut out on stalks, and nobody knows whom they portray.
King Sejong's scholars created the Korean alphabet, Hangul, in 1443.
It gave Korea its name, and in 1377 its monks printed a book with metal type.
Their language is the last survivor of those spoken in western Europe before the Indo-European languages arrived.
The first people of the Canary Islands; Silbo Gomero, the whistled language of La Gomera, is thought to come from them.
Celts who settled in central Anatolia; St Paul wrote them a letter.
By tradition Armenia was the first country to make Christianity its state religion, in 301.
Its kings controlled the gold that drew Portuguese traders inland.
They held off the Incas, and the Spanish never conquered them.
Upper Egypt's earliest farming culture, named after el-Badari, where it was found in the 1920s.
Egypt's last prehistoric culture, from which the first pharaohs emerged.
Saladin's family.
The Buddha's own people, who lived in the Himalayan foothills.
Herodotus says their queen Tomyris killed Cyrus the Great in battle, a tale that may be legend.
They spoke an Indo-European language in the oases of the Tarim Basin, far to the east of all its relatives.
Their name gave medieval Europe its word for China: Cathay.
They took northern China in 1127, and their descendants, renamed Manchus, founded the Qing.
Their kingdom of Western Xia fell to the Mongols in 1227, the year Genghis Khan died.
The poet Qu Yuan, remembered at the Dragon Boat Festival, served the kings of Chu.
Its kings built Borobudur and Prambanan.
Founded around 1400, it grew rich on the spice trade until the Portuguese took it in 1511.
Herodotus tells of their king Arganthonios, said to have reigned for 80 years.
Beowulf's people, from what is now southern Sweden.
Arminius of the Cherusci destroyed three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9.
Bohemia is named after them.
Paris is named after them.
Devon takes its name from them.
Greek myth put the Golden Fleece in Colchis, which was a real kingdom on the Black Sea.
Its scribes wrote one of the oldest known alphabets and left tablets listing its letters in order.
Some 17,000 clay tablets and fragments were found in its palace archives in the 1970s.
Named in an Assyrian inscription of 715 BC and in the Quran.
They mummified their dead some 2,000 years before the Egyptians did.
Never conquered by the Aztecs, they sided with Cortés in 1519.
Their latte stones, pillars topped with stone caps, once held up houses in the Mariana Islands.
A Saharan people of southern Libya who dug underground channels to tap water from beneath the desert.
Bronze Age Sardinians who left thousands of stone towers, the nuraghi, across their island.
A trading land centred on Bahrain. Sumerian myth made it a paradise, where the lion did not kill and the wolf took no lambs.
